rv.q: This version of Bull teaches us that accessibility cannot be an afterthought; it needs to be at the forefront of style and stagecraft.
All four actors are excellent, but Ciaran O'Breen, with his fluid, Rowan Atkinson-esque physicality, is outstanding as the hapless Thomas.
But the use of sign language brought an extra dimension to proceedings.
It may previously have won awards, but in a time of ubiquitous greed and corruption, I struggled to warm to the material.

Deafinitely Theatre makes the case for the magic and importance of BSL theatre being for all, and not as an afterthought, introducing me to a new type of theatre that lets language sing through the body.
It’s an idea which is drawn out perfectly by Garfield.
Bull may not be the show for you if you are looking for an upbeat storyline or something easy-going, but it is nonetheless well written, directed and delivered.
The production loses that hard-earned tension when David Sands’s Carter appears, a character who here becomes too large, losing the tension that sustained anticipation of his arrival has created.
Once again, Park Theatre has managed to put something genuinely different into its smaller Park90 space.

cn.t: Bartlett's brutal workplace drama remains unnerving in Deafinitely Theatre's BSL production, with critics praising the accessible staging and expressive signing, though some find the relentless bleakness difficult and pacing uneven.
